screens.title: What is IP routing?
screens.narratorSegment: Routing is the process of choosing paths across one or more networks so that data can travel from a source to a destination. At a basic level, routers inspect the destination IP address in a packet, consult a routing table that lists known networks and how to reach them, then forward the packet toward the appropriate next-hop or interface. Think of cities and road networks: each IP network is a city, and routers are the traffic controllers and signposts that send mail carriers toward the right city. A concrete example is a host on 10.0.0.0/24 that needs to reach 192.168.1.10; a router recognizes those as different networks and forwards the packet onto the next network hop, rather than switching it within the local VLAN. A common misconception is that every device somehow knows the entire internet — in reality, routers only know routes for directly connected networks, static entries you configure, and routes learned from dynamic protocols. If a route is missing and there's no default, the packet is dropped. This is why correct route distribution and default routes matter in design. As you learn routing, focus on how the routing table is a map and how the router uses that map every time it forwards a packet. How would you check whether a router knows the path to a remote web server?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Routing lets routers direct IP packets between networks using a routing table as a path map.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › What is IP routing?
Definition
Routing explained
Routing selects a path across multiple networks so packets can reach destinations outside the local network.
Example: Host on 10.0.0.0/24 sends to 192.168.1.10; router chooses next-hop toward that network.
Misconception: Routers know everything by default. Reality: routers only know configured, connected, or learned routes.
Why it matters: Missing routes or wrong masks can isolate hosts or services.
Key Takeaway

Routing maps are essential for inter-network reachability; the routing table is the router's map.

Analogy
Postal service: addresses correspond to IPs, cities to networks, and routers to sorting centers that read the address and forward to the next center toward the destination.
When routing is used
Any time a packet must leave its local IP network to reach a different network or the internet.
When switching suffices
When traffic stays inside the same broadcast domain and forwarding is done by MAC address.
Check your understanding
If a router has no route for a destination and no default route, what will happen to a packet destined for that address?

screens.title: Router versus Layer 2 switch
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference between a Layer 2 switch and a router is fundamental when designing or troubleshooting networks. A Layer 2 switch forwards frames based on MAC addresses and operates within a single broadcast domain or VLAN. It is optimized for local switching and does not make decisions based on IP addresses. In contrast, a router operates at Layer 3, forwards packets based on IP addresses, and connects different IP networks. A concrete scenario: when two hosts share a subnet, a switch forwards traffic between them without routing. But when hosts are in different subnets, a router must receive the packet and forward it to the correct network using its routing table. A common mistake is expecting a switch to forward traffic between subnets — unless it has Layer 3 capabilities, it will not. Even when switches support routing, dedicated routers typically handle more complex routing protocols and larger routing tables. Remember that the address types used for forwarding differ — MAC for switching, IP for routing — and that explains why routers are essential for inter-network reachability. How would you verify whether a device is switching or routing traffic in your environment?

keyIdea.title: Contrast
keyIdea.text: Switches forward by MAC within a LAN; routers forward by IP between networks. They serve complementary but distinct roles.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Router vs Switch
Comparison
Layer 2 Switch
Forwards frames based on MAC addresses inside a VLAN or broadcast domain.
Router
Forwards IP packets between networks using a routing table and longest prefix match.
Example: Two hosts on different subnets require routing; a switch alone cannot bridge their subnets unless it has Layer 3 features.
Misconception: All switches route between VLANs. Reality: Only Layer 3 switches or routers perform inter-subnet routing.
Practical check
To verify behavior, look at traffic that must cross subnets. If MAC learning tables suffice, switching is enough. If IP routing or route lookups occur, a router is involved.
Quick test: ping from one subnet to another and watch whether the router's route table shows the destination network.
Why it matters: Knowing which device performs routing informs where you configure access control, NAT, or route redistribution.

screens.title: Packet forwarding steps
screens.narratorSegment: When a router receives an IP packet, it follows a reliable sequence of steps before sending the packet onward. First, it inspects the destination IP address in the packet header to determine intent. Second, it consults its routing table and performs a longest prefix match to find the most specific route that applies to that destination. Third, once a matching routing table entry is selected, the router identifies the next-hop IP or the outgoing interface from the entry. Fourth, the router decrements the packet's Time-To-Live field — this prevents indefinite forwarding loops — and recalculates the IP header checksum to maintain integrity. Finally, the router encapsulates the packet in a new Layer 2 frame appropriate for the outgoing interface and transmits it. A concrete example: a packet to 192.168.1.10 matches 192.168.1.0/24, the route points to next-hop 10.0.0.1 via ge-0/0/0.0, TTL reduces by one and the packet egresses on ge-0/0/0.0. A frequent misconception is that preference values influence longest prefix matching — preference only matters when routes with identical prefixes are learned from different protocols. In troubleshooting, watch TTL-related ICMP messages or missing route entries as evidence of where forwarding stopped. How would you trace which hop discarded a packet in a multi-router path?

keyIdea.title: Forwarding sequence
keyIdea.text: Destination lookup → longest prefix match → select next-hop/interface → decrement TTL → recalculate checksum → egress.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Packet forwarding steps
Process Flow
1. Inspect destination
Read the destination IP from the packet header.
2. Longest prefix match
Find the most specific route in the routing table that matches the destination.
3. Select next-hop/interface
Determine the outgoing interface and next-hop IP from the chosen entry.
4. Update TTL and checksum
Decrement TTL and recalc IP header checksum to prevent loops.
5. Encapsulate and forward
Wrap in a Layer 2 frame suitable for the outgoing link and transmit.
Example walkthrough
Packet to 192.168.1.10: router finds 192.168.1.0/24 entry, next-hop 10.0.0.1 via ge-0/0/0.0, TTL decremented, checksum updated, egress on ge-0/0/0.0.
Common misconception: Preference values decide the route during prefix selection. Correction: Preference is used when multiple routes exist for the exact same prefix; longest prefix matching happens first.
Pro tip

Watch for TTL-expired ICMP messages to locate where packets are being dropped in a path.

screens.title: Routing table components
screens.narratorSegment: A routing table entry is more than a destination prefix; it contains the information a router needs to forward packets. The Destination Prefix specifies the network or host reachable via the entry, for example 192.168.1.0/24. The Next-Hop Address is the IP of the next router in the path, or it can indicate the route is directly connected. The Outgoing Interface tells the router which local interface to use when sending the packet to that next-hop. The Metric indicates the cost a dynamic routing protocol assigns to that path; lower metrics are usually preferred. Preference, also called administrative distance in other systems, ranks trustworthiness of routes learned from different sources — lower values are more trusted. Finally, the Protocol field records how the route was learned: Direct, Static, OSPF, BGP, and so on. A concrete Junos example shows 0.0.0.0/0 as a static route with preference 5 pointing via 192.168.1.1, while directly connected networks appear with preference 0. Misreading a mask or trusting a route from an unexpected protocol are common mistakes. When troubleshooting, read each component to understand why the router chose a route and whether it should be trusted.

keyIdea.title: Table anatomy
keyIdea.text: Destination, next-hop, outgoing interface, metric, preference and protocol together explain how a route is used for forwarding.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Routing table components
Definition
Destination Prefix — network or host reachable, e.g., 192.168.1.0/24.
Next-Hop Address — the next router IP or indication of directly connected.
Outgoing Interface — local interface used to forward the packet.
Metric — cost from a dynamic protocol; lower is preferred by that protocol.
Preference — administrative ranking of trustworthiness; lower is more trusted.
Protocol — how the route was learned: Direct, Static, OSPF, BGP, etc.
Scenario
Given a routing table entry, you can explain forwarding: a route to 10.0.0.0/24 via next-hop 192.168.1.1 on ge-0/0/0 means packets to 10.0.0.x are sent toward that next-hop on that interface.
Example: Default route 0.0.0.0/0 [Static/5] to 192.168.1.1 via ge-0/0/0.0 — used when no other specific match exists.
Mistake to avoid: Wrong subnet mask on a destination makes a route either too broad or too narrow, causing incorrect forwarding or unexpected drops.
Key Takeaway

Interpreting each field explains why a router chooses that route and whether it should be trusted in forwarding decisions.

screens.title: Preference vs Metric
screens.narratorSegment: Preference and metric are both values that help a router decide which route to use, but they serve different roles. Preference (also called administrative distance on other platforms) is a router-level trust value used to rank routes learned from different sources. Lower preference values indicate more trusted routes; for example, a directly connected route typically has preference 0, a static route might have preference 5, and some external OSPF routes can have much higher values. Metric, by contrast, is a path cost used by dynamic routing protocols to compare multiple paths to the same destination learned from the same protocol. For instance, OSPF uses interface bandwidth to compute cost metrics; lower metric indicates a preferred path within that protocol. Importantly, the router first selects the best route by longest prefix match; if multiple routes exist to the identical prefix from different sources, preference is used to choose among them. If several routes from the same protocol match, metrics come into play. A common misconception is to treat preference and metric interchangeably — preference compares sources and metric compares path cost inside a protocol. When you analyze route selection, inspect both fields to understand why a particular route is active.

keyIdea.title: Distinction
keyIdea.text: Preference ranks sources of routes; metric ranks paths within a routing protocol. Both influence final route selection in different stages.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Preference vs Metric
Definitions
Preference — a numerical trust value ranking where the route came from; lower is more trusted.
Metric — a protocol-specific path cost used by dynamic routing protocols to prefer one path over another.
Remember: Preference is considered only when multiple routes exist for the exact same prefix learned from different sources; metric is considered when comparing paths learned by the same protocol.
Examples & troubleshooting
Example: A static route with preference 5 and OSPF route with preference 10 to the same prefix — the static route is preferred. Example: Two OSPF-learned paths with metrics 10 and 20 — the metric 10 path is preferred by OSPF.
Practical check: If an unexpected route is active, verify whether a lower preference route exists or whether metric differences within the protocol favor a different path.
Common mistake: Changing metrics when you should adjust preference, or vice versa — use the appropriate value for the problem you're solving.
Key Takeaway

Preference ranks sources; metric ranks protocol path cost. Inspect both to understand active route selection.

screens.title: Static and dynamic routing
screens.narratorSegment: Static routing and dynamic routing are two approaches with different trade-offs. Static routes are manually configured by an administrator and remain fixed until changed. They are simple, predictable, and useful in small topologies or for default routes to an upstream provider. Dynamic routing uses protocols to exchange route information automatically between routers; this is preferable in larger or changing networks because routers learn and adapt to topology changes. A concrete scenario: use a static default route to point to a single ISP gateway in a small office; use dynamic protocols like OSPF or BGP in larger networks so routers can discover alternative paths and react to failures. A common pitfall is assuming dynamic routing will always be better — dynamic protocols introduce protocol overhead and complexity, and incorrect configuration can lead to route loops or unintended redistribution. Another common error is leaving a static route in place when the topology has changed, which can cause traffic to be sent toward an unreachable next-hop. When choosing between static and dynamic, weigh scale, control, and the operational overhead of maintaining routes. Static and dynamic routing means static routes are simple and predictable; dynamic routing scales and adapts to topology changes but requires protocol configuration and management.. In practical terms, when to configure static routes and when to rely on routing protocols. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: When to use each
keyIdea.text: Static routes are simple and predictable; dynamic routing scales and adapts to topology changes but requires protocol configuration and management.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Static vs Dynamic Routing
Comparison
Static — manually configured, no protocol overhead, predictable, best for small or fixed paths.
Dynamic — learned via protocols, adapts to topology changes, scales to larger networks.
Example: Small office uses a static default route to its ISP; a campus uses dynamic routing so routers discover alternative links after a failure.
Operational notes
Static routes require manual updates after topology changes. Dynamic protocols require correct metric and preference tuning to avoid undesired path selection.
Pitfall: A static route left configured after a link change can cause persistent black-holing of traffic.
Rule of thumb: Use static routes for simplicity when topology is stable; use dynamic routing when scale and resilience are required.
Key Takeaway

Choose static for control and simplicity; choose dynamic for scalability and automatic convergence after failures.

screens.title: Inspecting routes on Junos
screens.narratorSegment: On Junos devices you inspect routing information with show route from operational mode. You can also check a single prefix with show route 0.0.0.0/0 to confirm whether a default route is present. Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Inspecting routes on Junos
Command examples
Run these in operational mode to view routing information and filter by protocol or prefix.
user@router> show route
user@router> show route protocol direct
user@router> show route protocol static
user@router> show route 0.0.0.0/0
In output, + = active route, and lines show destination, preference/metric, and the next-hop or interface used for forwarding.
Sample output interpretation
Example snippet shows a default route 0.0.0.0/0 learned statically with preference 5 pointing to 192.168.1.1 via ge-0/0/0.0. A directly connected 10.0.0.0/24 appears with preference 0 and via ge-0/0/1.0. The active marker indicates the route currently used for forwarding.
Practical exercise: Run show route protocol direct and pick one route. Explain its destination, next-hop, preference and protocol to confirm forwarding behavior.
Mistake to avoid: Interpreting preference as a metric — preference ranks sources, not path cost.

screens.title: Common routing mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Two frequent causes of routing failures are missing routes and incorrect subnet masks. If a router has no route for a destination and no default route, it will drop the packet, often triggering a Destination Host Unreachable or an ICMP unreachable message. This happens because routers only know connected, static, or learned routes; they do not assume reachability. Misconfigured subnet masks create entries that are either too broad or too narrow, and that can result in packets being forwarded to the wrong next-hop or dropped. Another troubleshooting angle is to check preference and protocol: a route learned from an unexpected source might be less trustworthy, or a static route might be overriding a better dynamic path. Use show route and protocol filters to isolate routes, and inspect TTL or ICMP messages to find where a packet is stopped. A step-by-step debugging approach is to verify local interface addresses, confirm connected routes, check for a default route, and then examine static and dynamic entries to explain the forwarding choice. What single check would you run first to confirm the router knows where to send traffic to an external network?

Common issues
Missing route or default route causes packet drops to unreachable networks.
Incorrect subnet masks result in wrong route matches and misdirected traffic.
Unexpected route sources: verify preference and protocol to ensure the chosen route is trustworthy.

Start with connected routes and default route checks, then broaden to static and dynamic sources when a destination remains unreachable.

fullNarratorScript:
Routing is the system that lets separate IP networks exchange data. In this lesson you'll learn why routers matter, how they decide where a packet should go, and how to read the routing information that drives forwarding. Think of the internet as many cities and routers as the traffic controllers and road signs that guide each package to the right destination. You will see the core pieces that a router consults — destination prefix, next-hop, outgoing interface, metric and preference — and understand the role of the longest prefix match in choosing a path. We will also compare a Layer 2 switch and a router so you can tell when inter-network routing is required. Finally, you'll get a concrete Junos example of the show route output so you can inspect a real routing table. By the end of this module you will be more confident reading routing entries and understanding why an unexpected drop or a default route matters in everyday network troubleshooting. Consider how a single missing route could isolate an entire office; that is exactly what routing prevents when configured correctly.

These learning objectives define practical skills you will build. First, you'll be able to explain the fundamental purpose of IP routing — why it is needed to connect separate IP networks and ensure packets reach distant hosts. Second, you will learn to differentiate the role of a router from a Layer 2 switch: how a switch forwards frames by MAC addresses within a broadcast domain, and how a router forwards IP packets between networks. Third, you will describe the packet forwarding process a router follows when it receives an IP packet, including destination lookup, longest prefix matching, TTL decrement and checksum recalculation. Finally, you'll begin to identify the key elements of a routing table entry that a router uses to forward traffic. Each of these skills is tied to practical troubleshooting tasks, such as diagnosing why a host cannot reach a service, or why a route is not being used. These objectives will map directly to hands-on checks in Junos, like using show route and filtering by protocol or prefix to confirm what the router knows.

These additional objectives focus on applying and troubleshooting routing knowledge. You will learn to distinguish static routes, which are manually configured and remain fixed until changed, from dynamic routes that routers learn automatically through routing protocols. You will understand the purpose of a default route and when a router will drop a packet if it has no matching entry. You will also be able to interpret Junos route output and use simple show route filters to isolate direct or static routes. Together, these skills let you diagnose common mistakes such as missing default routes, incorrect subnet masks, or trusting a route learned from an unexpected protocol. Each objective ties back to practical checks you'll perform on a Junos device, and learning them will make everyday network troubleshooting faster and more precise.

Routing is the process of choosing paths across one or more networks so that data can travel from a source to a destination. At a basic level, routers inspect the destination IP address in a packet, consult a routing table that lists known networks and how to reach them, then forward the packet toward the appropriate next-hop or interface. Think of cities and road networks: each IP network is a city, and routers are the traffic controllers and signposts that send mail carriers toward the right city. A concrete example is a host on 10.0.0.0/24 that needs to reach 192.168.1.10; a router recognizes those as different networks and forwards the packet onto the next network hop, rather than switching it within the local VLAN. A common misconception is that every device somehow knows the entire internet — in reality, routers only know routes for directly connected networks, static entries you configure, and routes learned from dynamic protocols. If a route is missing and there's no default, the packet is dropped. This is why correct route distribution and default routes matter in design. As you learn routing, focus on how the routing table is a map and how the router uses that map every time it forwards a packet. How would you check whether a router knows the path to a remote web server?

Understanding the difference between a Layer 2 switch and a router is fundamental when designing or troubleshooting networks. A Layer 2 switch forwards frames based on MAC addresses and operates within a single broadcast domain or VLAN. It is optimized for local switching and does not make decisions based on IP addresses. In contrast, a router operates at Layer 3, forwards packets based on IP addresses, and connects different IP networks. A concrete scenario: when two hosts share a subnet, a switch forwards traffic between them without routing. But when hosts are in different subnets, a router must receive the packet and forward it to the correct network using its routing table. A common mistake is expecting a switch to forward traffic between subnets — unless it has Layer 3 capabilities, it will not. Even when switches support routing, dedicated routers typically handle more complex routing protocols and larger routing tables. Remember that the address types used for forwarding differ — MAC for switching, IP for routing — and that explains why routers are essential for inter-network reachability. How would you verify whether a device is switching or routing traffic in your environment?

When a router receives an IP packet, it follows a reliable sequence of steps before sending the packet onward. First, it inspects the destination IP address in the packet header to determine intent. Second, it consults its routing table and performs a longest prefix match to find the most specific route that applies to that destination. Third, once a matching routing table entry is selected, the router identifies the next-hop IP or the outgoing interface from the entry. Fourth, the router decrements the packet's Time-To-Live field — this prevents indefinite forwarding loops — and recalculates the IP header checksum to maintain integrity. Finally, the router encapsulates the packet in a new Layer 2 frame appropriate for the outgoing interface and transmits it. A concrete example: a packet to 192.168.1.10 matches 192.168.1.0/24, the route points to next-hop 10.0.0.1 via ge-0/0/0.0, TTL reduces by one and the packet egresses on ge-0/0/0.0. A frequent misconception is that preference values influence longest prefix matching — preference only matters when routes with identical prefixes are learned from different protocols. In troubleshooting, watch TTL-related ICMP messages or missing route entries as evidence of where forwarding stopped. How would you trace which hop discarded a packet in a multi-router path?

A routing table entry is more than a destination prefix; it contains the information a router needs to forward packets. The Destination Prefix specifies the network or host reachable via the entry, for example 192.168.1.0/24. The Next-Hop Address is the IP of the next router in the path, or it can indicate the route is directly connected. The Outgoing Interface tells the router which local interface to use when sending the packet to that next-hop. The Metric indicates the cost a dynamic routing protocol assigns to that path; lower metrics are usually preferred. Preference, also called administrative distance in other systems, ranks trustworthiness of routes learned from different sources — lower values are more trusted. Finally, the Protocol field records how the route was learned: Direct, Static, OSPF, BGP, and so on. A concrete Junos example shows 0.0.0.0/0 as a static route with preference 5 pointing via 192.168.1.1, while directly connected networks appear with preference 0. Misreading a mask or trusting a route from an unexpected protocol are common mistakes. When troubleshooting, read each component to understand why the router chose a route and whether it should be trusted.

Preference and metric are both values that help a router decide which route to use, but they serve different roles. Preference (also called administrative distance on other platforms) is a router-level trust value used to rank routes learned from different sources. Lower preference values indicate more trusted routes; for example, a directly connected route typically has preference 0, a static route might have preference 5, and some external OSPF routes can have much higher values. Metric, by contrast, is a path cost used by dynamic routing protocols to compare multiple paths to the same destination learned from the same protocol. For instance, OSPF uses interface bandwidth to compute cost metrics; lower metric indicates a preferred path within that protocol. Importantly, the router first selects the best route by longest prefix match; if multiple routes exist to the identical prefix from different sources, preference is used to choose among them. If several routes from the same protocol match, metrics come into play. A common misconception is to treat preference and metric interchangeably — preference compares sources and metric compares path cost inside a protocol. When you analyze route selection, inspect both fields to understand why a particular route is active.

Static routing and dynamic routing are two approaches with different trade-offs. Static routes are manually configured by an administrator and remain fixed until changed. They are simple, predictable, and useful in small topologies or for default routes to an upstream provider. Dynamic routing uses protocols to exchange route information automatically between routers; this is preferable in larger or changing networks because routers learn and adapt to topology changes. A concrete scenario: use a static default route to point to a single ISP gateway in a small office; use dynamic protocols like OSPF or BGP in larger networks so routers can discover alternative paths and react to failures. A common pitfall is assuming dynamic routing will always be better — dynamic protocols introduce protocol overhead and complexity, and incorrect configuration can lead to route loops or unintended redistribution. Another common error is leaving a static route in place when the topology has changed, which can cause traffic to be sent toward an unreachable next-hop. When choosing between static and dynamic, weigh scale, control, and the operational overhead of maintaining routes. Static and dynamic routing means static routes are simple and predictable; dynamic routing scales and adapts to topology changes but requires protocol configuration and management.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
